purpose: Execution of chapter 7 of the UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts (2016 edition): non-performance in general (art. 7.1.1–7.1.7), the right to performance (art. 7.2.1–7.2.5), termination of the contract and its effects (art. 7.3.1–7.3.7), damages and interest (art. 7.4.1–7.4.13). The types for party, contract, term and the organ of evaluative elements come from the hub `unidroit.picc`. This is the package where the comparison with the 1980 UN Convention is densest: fundamental non-performance, the right to cure and the rate of interest are arranged differently from articles 25, 48 and 78 of the Convention. The list of questions and boundaries is in analysis/questions.json and QUESTIONS.md.
limitations: THIS IS NOT THE LAW OF A STATE. The Principles apply when the parties have agreed on them, or when a court or arbitral tribunal takes them as general principles of law; they do not replace the mandatory rules of the applicable law (article 1.4, hub `unidroit.picc`).

THE SOURCE NAMES THE RATE OF INTEREST, NOT THE NUMBER. Article 7.4.9(2) gives a RULE OF CHOICE in three steps (the bank rate at the place for payment, the same rate in the state of the currency of payment, the rate under the law of that state); the value of the rate is brought by the case. Article 78 of the Convention names not even a rule — and that is what the Principles answer under article 7(2) of the Convention.

FUNDAMENTAL NON-PERFORMANCE IS NOT A DEFINITION HERE BUT FIVE CIRCUMSTANCES (article 7.3.1(2)), the fifth of which — disproportionate loss to the non-performing party — works AGAINST termination. Article 25 of the Convention is built differently: one definition with foreseeability. The instruments answer differently on the same facts, and this is observed by case 03.

THE EVALUATIVE ELEMENTS OF CHAPTER 7 GO THROUGH THE §47.3 JUDGMENT CHANNEL with the organ `Tribunal`: the appropriateness of cure and a legitimate interest in refusing it (7.1.4), a reasonable additional period (7.1.5), the gross unfairness of invoking an exemption clause (7.1.6), the unforeseeability and insurmountability of an impediment (7.1.7), an unreasonably burdensome performance and its availability from another source (7.2.2), substantial deprivation of what was expected and disproportionate loss (7.3.1), a reasonable belief in a future fundamental non-performance (7.3.4), foreseeability of the harm (7.4.4), the reasonableness of the place taken as a benchmark for the current price (7.4.6), the appropriateness of the currency of the harm (7.4.12), and a grossly excessive agreed sum (7.4.13).

THE MODEL DOES NOT COMPUTE THE AMOUNT OF DAMAGES: articles 7.4.2–7.4.7 name WHAT is recoverable and what limits it, while the numbers (the difference in prices, the contribution of the aggrieved party, the amount of interest) are brought by the case. The proportion for the loss of a chance (7.4.3(2)) is left to the court for the same reason.

ARTICLES 7.3.6 AND 7.3.7 ON RESTITUTION REFER TO SEPARATE REGIMES for contracts to be performed at one time and for long-term contracts to be performed over a period of time. Which one is before us is a fact of the case, not a conclusion of the model.
